title: Pressure and normal force
prior_knowledge_summary: Density is mass per unit volume.
Use density equals mass divided by volume and convert volume units consistently.
Weight is a downward force, and a force can be resolved into perpendicular components.
new_learning: Define pressure as normal force per unit area.
Use p = F/A and rearrange it for force or area.
Use the total contact area and the force normal to the surface.
Convert contact areas and pressure units before substitution.

visual_planning.reason: Six planned visuals separate contact area, normal direction, symbol meaning, unit conversion, rearrangement and force balance. Asset generation is outside this bounded four-file package.
visual_planning.style: landscape 3:2 rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Why does one shoe sink further?
content: Imagine the same student standing first on a narrow heel and then on a wide snowshoe. The downward force is almost unchanged, yet the narrow heel sinks further into soft ground.
The puzzle is not only how large the force is. We also need to know how much surface shares that force. This leads to pressure.

figure.purpose: Create a prediction about equal force acting over unequal contact areas
figure.brief: Landscape teacher sketch with the same student represented by the same downward force arrow in two panels. One panel shows a narrow heel making a deep mark in soft ground; the other shows a wide snowshoe making a shallow mark. Do not write a pressure formula.
figure.alt_text: The same downward force acts through a narrow heel and a wide snowshoe, producing different impressions in soft ground.

blocks.title: Area changes how concentrated a force is
content: Suppose a 600 N normal force is spread over 0.030 m². If the contact area is halved while the force stays 600 N, each square metre must carry twice as much force.
So a smaller contact area gives a larger pressure for the same normal force. A larger contact area gives a smaller pressure.

figure.purpose: Show inverse scaling between contact area and pressure
figure.brief: Two equal 600 N downward arrows above contact patches of 0.030 m squared and 0.015 m squared. Use equal-size grid cells beneath each patch to show that the second force is shared by half as many cells. Label only the given force and areas plus 'pressure doubles'.
figure.alt_text: An equal normal force is shared over a full contact patch and a patch with half the area.

blocks.title: Pressure uses the normal force
content: The accepted definition is: normal force per unit area.
Normal means perpendicular to the surface. A force parallel to a surface may cause sliding, but it does not contribute to pressure on that surface.
The normal force is the contact force pressing one surface against the other. It is not automatically equal to weight. Other upward or downward forces can change it.

figure.purpose: Separate the normal force from a force parallel to the contact surface
figure.brief: Draw a block on a horizontal surface with one arrow perpendicular to the surface labelled 'normal component' and one arrow along the surface labelled 'parallel component'. Highlight only the perpendicular arrow as contributing to pressure.
figure.alt_text: A force is split into a component perpendicular to a surface and a component parallel to it.

blocks.title: The formula to remember
content: Remember p = F/A. Here p is pressure in pascals, F is the force normal to the surface in newtons, and A is the total contact area in square metres.
One pascal is one newton per square metre, so 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻². Pressure also has SI base units kg m⁻¹ s⁻².
Useful conversions are 1 kPa = 10³ Pa, 1 MPa = 10⁶ Pa, 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m² and 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m². Area conversions square the length conversion.

blocks.title: From force and area to pressure
content: A flat support pushes normally on a panel with force 270 N over an area of 0.0150 m².
Check independently by reversing the calculation: pA = 18 000 × 0.0150 = 270 N. The units also reduce to N m⁻², which is Pa.

figure.purpose: Teach substitution, pressure units and a reverse check
figure.brief: Annotated worked layout with a 270 N normal arrow, a 0.0150 m squared contact patch, the substitution p = 270 divided by 0.0150, conversion to 18.0 kPa, and a separate reverse-check box showing pA = 270 N.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout calculates pressure from 270 newtons and 0.0150 square metres, then checks the force.

blocks.title: Finding the required contact area
content: A clamp must apply 560 N normally without exceeding a uniform pressure of 2.80 × 10⁵ Pa. Rearrange before substituting: A = F/p.
A = 560/(2.80 × 10⁵) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ m². This is 20.0 cm² because 1 m² = 10⁴ cm².
A smaller area would produce a pressure above the limit. A larger area would reduce the pressure, so the direction of the result is physically sensible.

figure.brief: Three-step hand-drawn sequence: write A = F divided by p, substitute 560 N and 2.80 times 10 to the power 5 Pa, then convert 2.00 times 10 to the power minus 3 m squared to 20.0 cm squared using an area conversion grid.
figure.alt_text: A three-step calculation finds a contact area and converts square metres to square centimetres.

blocks.title: Find the normal force before using pressure
content: A display platform has weight 840 N and is lifted upward by a cable with vertical force 120 N while it remains at rest on the floor. The floor does not carry the full 840 N.
Vertical equilibrium gives normal force + 120 = 840, so the normal force is 720 N. If the total floor contact area is 0.0240 m², then p = 720/0.0240 = 30 000 Pa = 30.0 kPa.
The cable removes some of the load from the floor. This is why using 840 N directly would overestimate the pressure. Check: the three vertical forces sum to zero, and 30 000 × 0.0240 = 720 N.

figure.purpose: Connect force balance to the normal force used in the pressure formula
figure.brief: Two-panel teacher sketch. First panel: free-body diagram of a platform with 840 N down, 120 N cable force up and unknown normal force up. Second panel: calculation flow from N + 120 = 840 to N = 720 N and p = 30.0 kPa over 0.0240 m squared.
figure.alt_text: A platform's upward cable force reduces the normal force on the floor before pressure is calculated.

blocks.title: Force, weight and pressure are not interchangeable
content: It feels natural to use an object's weight as F because weight often presses an object onto a horizontal floor. That shortcut fails when another force has a vertical component, or when the surface is not horizontal.
First identify the contact surface. Then find the component of contact force perpendicular to it. Finally divide by the total area actually touching the surface.
Another common error is to use the area of one foot or pad when several identical contacts share the force. Add all contact areas before calculating the average uniform pressure.

blocks.title: A reliable pressure routine
content: Mark the contact surface and the perpendicular direction. Find the normal force, using force balance if needed. Convert the total contact area to m² and pressure to Pa. Choose p = F/A or the required rearrangement.
Finish with a direction check: for the same force, a smaller area must give a larger pressure. A calculation involving depth in a liquid belongs to the next lessons, not this one.

total contact area across multiple pads

assuming normal force always equals weight
using one contact pad's area instead of total contact area
converting lengths but not squaring the area conversion
